segments.heading: Abstract / Introduction
segments.text: Motor complication in immunocompetent individuals with varicella zoster virus (VZV) reactivation is uncommon and may mimic a compressive spinal disorder.

segments.heading: Abstract / Case Presentation
segments.text: A 77‐year‐old immunocompetent woman presented with an acute left foot drop preceded by coryzal symptoms and lower back pain. A vesicular rash developed over the left foot one week after the weakness began. Examination showed a predominantly severe left ankle dorsiflexion weakness with reduced sensation over the L5 and S1 dermatomes. A noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral spine showed noncompressive degenerative changes. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, a reduced CSF‐to‐serum glucose ratio, and isolated VZV DNA on the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). VZV DNA was also detected from a vesicle swab. She received 14 days of intravenous acyclovir with neuropathic analgesia. A nerve conduction study and electromyography (NCS/EMG) at three months showed a severe left common peroneal neuropathy with sciatic nerve involvement. There was an initial slow motor recovery with persisting neuropathic pain, but only a residual moderate ankle dorsiflexion weakness remained at 9 months.

segments.heading: Abstract / Discussion
segments.text: The combination of preceding radicular pain, vesicular rash, significant leg weakness, and positive VZV DNA in CSF and vesicle specimen supported a diagnosis of VZV‐associated meningoradiculitis. The NCS/EMG was consistent with an evolution of VZV involvement at multiple neuraxial levels into a predominantly peripheral neuropathy. This diagnosis is easily missed when radicular pain precedes or occurs without a rash and when imaging is disproportionate to the severity of deficit. CSF PCR and skin lesion sampling are central to an early diagnosis.

segments.heading: Abstract / Conclusion
segments.text: VZV should be considered in patients with acute painful radiculopathy with significant limb weakness that is out of proportion to imaging findings, even without immunosuppression or an early rash. Early antiviral therapy can limit disability, although residual neurological deficits and pain may persist.

segments.heading: 1. Introduction
segments.text: Varicella zoster virus (VZV) reactivation typically presents as a painful dermatomal rash (herpes zoster), but peripheral nervous system involvement such as sciatic or common peroneal neuropathy is uncommon, especially in immunocompetent individuals. We report an elderly woman with VZV‐associated meningoradiculitis to emphasize the diagnostic challenges and importance of early antiviral therapy.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: A 77‐year‐old woman with a background history of hypertension, knee osteoarthritis, and osteoporosis presented to the emergency department (ED) with acute left foot weakness. Three weeks before admission, she developed low‐grade fever, headache, and coryzal symptoms shortly after receiving an influenza vaccination. These symptoms resolved, but she subsequently experienced persistent left lower back pain and leg cramps. One week prior to admission, she was assessed and initially diagnosed with lower back strain in the ED visit and was discharged with oral analgesics. Weakness of left ankle dorsiflexion began at about this time, approximately one week before the rash appeared. A day before the current admission, she developed numbness and itchy rashes with small blisters over the dorsum of her left foot. There was no history of preceding trauma, constitutional symptoms, or incontinence. She recalled a history of chickenpox infection during adolescence but was not on any immunosuppressant. A timeline of the clinical course is provided in Table 1.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There were clusters of vesicular rashes over the left lateral shin, dorsum of foot, and left big toe, consistent with a dermatomal distribution (Figure 1). The cranial nerves and upper limbs were normal. The tone was normal in the lower limbs. There was a severe weakness in the left ankle dorsiflexion with Medical Research Council (MRC) Grade 0, moderate weakness of ankle plantar flexion/inversion and eversion (MRC Grade 3), and mild weakness affecting the left hip flexion/knee flexion and extension (MRC Grade 4). There was a reduced left ankle jerk but normal knee jerks. Plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. There was reduced pinprick sensation over L5 and S1 dermatomes. There was no cerebellar sign.

There was a severe weakness in the left ankle dorsiflexion with Medical Research Council (MRC) Grade 0, moderate weakness of ankle plantar flexion/inversion and eversion (MRC Grade 3), and mild weakness affecting the left hip flexion/knee flexion and extension (MRC Grade 4). There was a reduced left ankle jerk but normal knee jerks. Plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. There was reduced pinprick sensation over L5 and S1 dermatomes. There was no cerebellar sign.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were within normal limits. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was mildly raised at 38 mm/hr (reference < 20 mm/hr) and C‐reactive protein at 8.2 mg/L (< 3.0 mg/L).

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was unremarkable. A noncontrast MRI of the lumbosacral spine demonstrated degenerative spondylotic changes most pronounced at L4‐L5 and L5‐S1, with mild right and moderate left exit foramina narrowing. There was no neural compression to explain the severity of the foot drop.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: A lumbar puncture was performed with a normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure of 18 cm H_(2)O. CSF analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis (155 cells/mm3, 80% lymphocytes, and 20% neutrophils), elevated protein of 1.67 g/L, and reduced CSF/serum glucose ratio of 0.47 (CSF glucose 2.7 mmol/L; serum glucose 5.7 mmol/L). CSF culture was negative, and oligoclonal bands were not detected. CSF acid‐fast bacillus (AFB) smear was negative. AFB culture was not performed due to insufficient sample volume. A multiplex meningitis/encephalitis polymerase chain reaction (PCR) panel (BioFire FilmArray) of the CSF was negative for all targets except VZV. VZV DNA was subsequently detected from a skin swab of the foot vesicles, confirming the diagnosis of VZV reactivation.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: In view of the acute radicular pain, dermatomal vesicular eruption, lower motor neurone pattern weakness affecting multiple left leg muscle groups, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, and positive VZV PCR, a diagnosis of VZV‐associated meningoradiculitis was initially made. After discussion with the infectious diseases team, she was treated with intravenous acyclovir for 2 weeks in accordance with institutional protocol for VZV infection involving the nervous system. She was commenced on analgesia for neuropathic pain. She was then transferred to a rehabilitation ward for intensive physiotherapy and gait training.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: A nerve conduction study and electromyography (NCS/EMG) was performed 3 months after symptom onset. This demonstrated a severe left common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head with sciatic nerve involvement, without electrophysiological evidence of L5 radiculopathy. Needle EMG of the left tibialis anterior revealed acute spontaneous responses with polyphasic discrete motor unit action potentials, suggesting residual axon continuity as well as ongoing renervation.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: At five‐month outpatient review follow‐up, there was an improvement in gait, though the neuropathic pain persisted, requiring symptomatic pharmacological therapy.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: At nine months, her lower limb strength had returned to full power in all muscle groups except ankle dorsiflexion, which remained at MRC Grade 3. She continued physiotherapy and was referred to occupational therapy for a nighttime ankle foot orthosis.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: The combination of an acute painful lumbar syndrome with a predominantly dense unilateral foot drop raised several diagnostic possibilities, which were considered and excluded as follows.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: A compressive L5‐S1 radiculopathy or lumbar disc herniation was the initial working diagnosis, given the preceding back pain and the degenerative changes seen on imaging. However, the noncontrast MRI of the lumbosacral spine did not show neural compression proportionate to a complete (MRC Grade 0) foot drop.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: A compressive common peroneal palsy at the fibular head, for example, from prolonged bed rest or leg positioning during the acute illness, could not be entirely excluded and may have been contributory; however, it does not account for the preceding dermatomal pain, the CSF pleocytosis, or the positive VZV PCR.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: Other causes of lumbosacral plexopathy were considered unlikely. There was no biochemical evidence of diabetes mellitus, making an associated lumbosacral radiculoplexoneuropathy improbable. A neoplastic or infiltrative process was not supported, given the absence of constitutional symptoms, normal hematological and CSF cytology results, and clinical improvement after acyclovir and rehabilitation. An acute inflammatory neuropathy such as Guillain–Barre syndrome was also unlikely, as the deficit was strictly focal and asymmetric, and the CSF showed lymphocytic pleocytosis rather than albuminocytological dissociation.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: Finally, a bacterial, tuberculous, or fungal meningitis was considered because of the reduced CSF‐to‐serum glucose ratio, but CSF culture was negative. The multiplex meningitis/encephalitis PCR panel was negative for all six bacterial targets and for Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii. CSF AFB smear was negative. AFB culture was not performed due to insufficient sample volume. Tuberculous meningitis was in any case considered unlikely given the absence of fever or constitutional symptoms, the absence of tuberculosis risk factors, the acute rather than subacute course, the only mildly reduced glucose ratio (0.47), and the detection of an alternative pathogen in both CSF and skin.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: The detection of VZV DNA in both the CSF and a vesicle swab, together with the clinical response to acyclovir, confirmed and supported VZV as the sole identified etiology.

segments.heading: 2. Case Report
segments.text: The NCS/EMG at 3‐month follow‐up localized the lesion to the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head with sciatic nerve involvement rather than to a lumbar nerve root, supporting a predominantly peripheral process rather than root compression.

segments.heading: 3. Discussion
segments.text: This case illustrates VZV reactivation presenting as meningoradiculitis with an evolving sciatic and common peroneal neuropathy in an immunocompetent elderly woman, initially mimicking a mechanical lumbar polyradiculopathy. Although VZV reactivation usually presents as a painful dermatomal vesicular eruption (herpes zoster), motor complications are relatively uncommon and are easily missed when the rash is delayed or absent (zoster sine herpete).

segments.heading: 3. Discussion
segments.text: The initial clinical syndrome was most consistent with VZV‐associated meningoradiculitis, given the severe radicular pain preceding the rash, dermatomal zoster eruption, lower motor neurone pattern weakness affecting different muscle groups in the left leg, inflammatory CSF abnormalities, and detection of VZV DNA in the CSF.

segments.heading: 3. Discussion
segments.text: A literature review identified only seven previously reported cases of VZV‐associated sciatic neuropathy with common peroneal neuropathy (Table 2). Although such motor involvement is classically described in immunocompromised patients, it also occurs in immunocompetent individuals [–], and immunosenescence is thought to increase this risk in older adults. In a recent cohort of patients with VZV DNA detected in the CSF, the neurological syndromes and outcomes were heterogeneous [].
segments.text_with_reference_markers: A literature review identified only seven previously reported cases of VZV‐associated sciatic neuropathy with common peroneal neuropathy (Table [TABLE:tbl-0002 2] ). Although such motor involvement is classically described in immunocompromised patients, it also occurs in immunocompetent individuals [ [BIBR:bib-0001 1] – [BIBR:bib-0005 5] ], and immunosenescence is thought to increase this risk in older adults. In a recent cohort of patients with VZV DNA detected in the CSF, the neurological syndromes and outcomes were heterogeneous [ [BIBR:bib-0006 6] ].

segments.heading: 3. Discussion
segments.text: The neurological complications of VZV are broad, ranging from postherpetic neuralgia to meningoencephalitis and myelitis. Motor involvement, termed zoster paresis or segmental zoster paresis, occurs in a minority of patients [–]. In our patient, an acute lower back pain radiating to the leg preceded the rash and led to an initial diagnosis of musculoskeletal strain, consistent with reports that zoster radiculopathy can present with dermatomal pain before the rash and be confused with compressive lumbar disease [].

Motor involvement, termed zoster paresis or segmental zoster paresis, occurs in a minority of patients [ [BIBR:bib-0007 7] – [BIBR:bib-0009 9] ]. In our patient, an acute lower back pain radiating to the leg preceded the rash and led to an initial diagnosis of musculoskeletal strain, consistent with reports that zoster radiculopathy can present with dermatomal pain before the rash and be confused with compressive lumbar disease [ [BIBR:bib-0010 10] ].

segments.heading: 3. Discussion
segments.text: The rash may also be atypical. Leo et al. described a 79‐year‐old woman with sciatica and foot drop followed several days later by an atypical petechial rash in the L4‐L5 distribution, underscoring that both the timing and the morphology of the rash may be nonclassical in VZV‐related sciatic neuropathy [].

segments.heading: 3. Discussion
segments.text: A limitation of our case is the use of noncontrast lumbosacral MRI. Even though the appearance of mild degenerative changes and the mismatch between these findings and the severe neurological deficit had prompted further investigations, use of contrast‐enhanced MRI could have potentially revealed enhancement of affected nerve roots, plexus, or peripheral nerves. This would enable a better characterization of the full extent of the neuroanatomy being affected. This is supported by a previous report showing that contrast‐enhanced MRI can demonstrate nerve root or sciatic nerve enhancement in segmental zoster paresis [].

segments.heading: 3. Discussion
segments.text: Neurophysiological testing was deferred during the acute admission for practical and infection control reasons. This is relevant because NCS/EMG performed within the first one to two weeks may be normal or nonlocalizing before denervation is established. The NCS/EMG for our patient at three months nonetheless confirmed a severe left common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head with sciatic nerve involvement, without electrophysiological evidence of L5 radiculopathy, supporting a predominantly peripheral distribution of established injury rather than root compression.

segments.heading: 3. Discussion
segments.text: Herpes zoster radiculopathy that mimics disc herniation both clinically and electrophysiologically has also been described in a previous case report []. Similar patterns have been described in case reports of segmental zoster paresis and VZV‐associated lumbosacral radiculoplexoneuropathy [, ], where initial radicular pain and imaging findings are followed by electrodiagnostic evidence of plexus or peripheral nerve involvement. We postulated that the initial severe radicular pain in our patient signified the meningeal and nerve root inflammation in the early phase of illness. The subsequent NCS/EMG had only revealed the residual, predominantly peripheral component of the injury and not the initial polyradiculitis after the completion of the course of acyclovir. This final localization with predominantly peripheral nerve involvement also reflects the distribution of established axonal injury, rather than excluding possible earlier proximal or root‐level inflammation.
segments.text_with_reference_markers: Herpes zoster radiculopathy that mimics disc herniation both clinically and electrophysiologically has also been described in a previous case report [ [BIBR:bib-0012 12] ]. Similar patterns have been described in case reports of segmental zoster paresis and VZV‐associated lumbosacral radiculoplexoneuropathy [ [BIBR:bib-0008 8] , [BIBR:bib-0009 9] ], where initial radicular pain and imaging findings are followed by electrodiagnostic evidence of plexus or peripheral nerve involvement. We postulated that the initial severe radicular pain in our patient signified the meningeal and nerve root inflammation in the early phase of illness. The subsequent NCS/EMG had only revealed the residual, predominantly peripheral component of the injury and not the initial polyradiculitis after the completion of the course of acyclovir. This final localization with predominantly peripheral nerve involvement also reflects the distribution of established axonal injury, rather than excluding possible earlier proximal or root‐level inflammation.

segments.heading: 3. Discussion
segments.text: The profound foot drop reflects the pathophysiology of VZV reactivation in the dorsal root ganglion, with spread to the ventral roots, anterior horn cells, or plexus, producing inflammatory neuritis, demyelination, or neuronal loss. VZV neurotropism can also cause vascular invasion, leading to ischemic neuropathy or perineuritis []. Severe lumbosacral VZV involvement can present as sciatica with motor loss and even hemi‐cauda equina syndrome []. Corticosteroids have been combined with antivirals to limit this inflammatory response in some reports, although our patient recovered with intravenous acyclovir alone.

segments.text: The 14‐day course of intravenous acyclovir was selected according to our institutional protocol for VZV infection involving the nervous system. Across reported cases, early antiviral therapy with supportive neurorehabilitation is consistently emphasized, although outcomes vary and residual deficits are common. The early intravenous acyclovir and rehabilitation produced early gait improvement despite residual weakness in our patient. She had persistent ankle dorsiflexion weakness (MRC Grade 3) at nine months follow up, requiring continued physiotherapy and ankle foot orthosis. This underscores that even with timely treatment, VZV infection can result in long term focal deficits, as reported in cases of segmental zoster paresis [].

text:
[b00001] Abstract / Introduction
Motor complication in immunocompetent individuals with varicella zoster virus (VZV) reactivation is uncommon and may mimic a compressive spinal disorder.

[b00002] Abstract / Case Presentation
A 77‐year‐old immunocompetent woman presented with an acute left foot drop preceded by coryzal symptoms and lower back pain. A vesicular rash developed over the left foot one week after the weakness began. Examination showed a predominantly severe left ankle dorsiflexion weakness with reduced sensation over the L5 and S1 dermatomes. A noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral spine showed noncompressive degenerative changes. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, a reduced CSF‐to‐serum glucose ratio, and isolated VZV DNA on the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). VZV DNA was also detected from a vesicle swab. She received 14 days of intravenous acyclovir with neuropathic analgesia. A nerve conduction study and electromyography (NCS/EMG) at three months showed a severe left common peroneal neuropathy with sciatic nerve involvement. There was an initial slow motor recovery with persisting neuropathic pain, but only a residual moderate ankle dorsiflexion weakness remained at 9 months.

[b00003] Abstract / Discussion
The combination of preceding radicular pain, vesicular rash, significant leg weakness, and positive VZV DNA in CSF and vesicle specimen supported a diagnosis of VZV‐associated meningoradiculitis. The NCS/EMG was consistent with an evolution of VZV involvement at multiple neuraxial levels into a predominantly peripheral neuropathy. This diagnosis is easily missed when radicular pain precedes or occurs without a rash and when imaging is disproportionate to the severity of deficit. CSF PCR and skin lesion sampling are central to an early diagnosis.

[b00004] Abstract / Conclusion
VZV should be considered in patients with acute painful radiculopathy with significant limb weakness that is out of proportion to imaging findings, even without immunosuppression or an early rash. Early antiviral therapy can limit disability, although residual neurological deficits and pain may persist.

[b00005] 1. Introduction
Varicella zoster virus (VZV) reactivation typically presents as a painful dermatomal rash (herpes zoster), but peripheral nervous system involvement such as sciatic or common peroneal neuropathy is uncommon, especially in immunocompetent individuals. We report an elderly woman with VZV‐associated meningoradiculitis to emphasize the diagnostic challenges and importance of early antiviral therapy.

[b00006] 2. Case Report
A 77‐year‐old woman with a background history of hypertension, knee osteoarthritis, and osteoporosis presented to the emergency department (ED) with acute left foot weakness. Three weeks before admission, she developed low‐grade fever, headache, and coryzal symptoms shortly after receiving an influenza vaccination. These symptoms resolved, but she subsequently experienced persistent left lower back pain and leg cramps. One week prior to admission, she was assessed and initially diagnosed with lower back strain in the ED visit and was discharged with oral analgesics. Weakness of left ankle dorsiflexion began at about this time, approximately one week before the rash appeared. A day before the current admission, she developed numbness and itchy rashes with small blisters over the dorsum of her left foot. There was no history of preceding trauma, constitutional symptoms, or incontinence. She recalled a history of chickenpox infection during adolescence but was not on any immunosuppressant. A timeline of the clinical course is provided in Table 1.

[b00016] 2. Case Report
On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There were clusters of vesicular rashes over the left lateral shin, dorsum of foot, and left big toe, consistent with a dermatomal distribution (Figure 1). The cranial nerves and upper limbs were normal. The tone was normal in the lower limbs. There was a severe weakness in the left ankle dorsiflexion with Medical Research Council (MRC) Grade 0, moderate weakness of ankle plantar flexion/inversion and eversion (MRC Grade 3), and mild weakness affecting the left hip flexion/knee flexion and extension (MRC Grade 4). There was a reduced left ankle jerk but normal knee jerks. Plantar responses were flexor bilaterally. There was reduced pinprick sensation over L5 and S1 dermatomes. There was no cerebellar sign.

[b00017] 2. Case Report
Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were within normal limits. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was mildly raised at 38 mm/hr (reference < 20 mm/hr) and C‐reactive protein at 8.2 mg/L (< 3.0 mg/L).

[b00018] 2. Case Report
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was unremarkable. A noncontrast MRI of the lumbosacral spine demonstrated degenerative spondylotic changes most pronounced at L4‐L5 and L5‐S1, with mild right and moderate left exit foramina narrowing. There was no neural compression to explain the severity of the foot drop.

[b00019] 2. Case Report
A lumbar puncture was performed with a normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure of 18 cm H_(2)O. CSF analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis (155 cells/mm3, 80% lymphocytes, and 20% neutrophils), elevated protein of 1.67 g/L, and reduced CSF/serum glucose ratio of 0.47 (CSF glucose 2.7 mmol/L; serum glucose 5.7 mmol/L). CSF culture was negative, and oligoclonal bands were not detected. CSF acid‐fast bacillus (AFB) smear was negative. AFB culture was not performed due to insufficient sample volume. A multiplex meningitis/encephalitis polymerase chain reaction (PCR) panel (BioFire FilmArray) of the CSF was negative for all targets except VZV. VZV DNA was subsequently detected from a skin swab of the foot vesicles, confirming the diagnosis of VZV reactivation.

[b00020] 2. Case Report
In view of the acute radicular pain, dermatomal vesicular eruption, lower motor neurone pattern weakness affecting multiple left leg muscle groups, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, and positive VZV PCR, a diagnosis of VZV‐associated meningoradiculitis was initially made. After discussion with the infectious diseases team, she was treated with intravenous acyclovir for 2 weeks in accordance with institutional protocol for VZV infection involving the nervous system. She was commenced on analgesia for neuropathic pain. She was then transferred to a rehabilitation ward for intensive physiotherapy and gait training.

[b00021] 2. Case Report
A nerve conduction study and electromyography (NCS/EMG) was performed 3 months after symptom onset. This demonstrated a severe left common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head with sciatic nerve involvement, without electrophysiological evidence of L5 radiculopathy. Needle EMG of the left tibialis anterior revealed acute spontaneous responses with polyphasic discrete motor unit action potentials, suggesting residual axon continuity as well as ongoing renervation.

[b00022] 2. Case Report
At five‐month outpatient review follow‐up, there was an improvement in gait, though the neuropathic pain persisted, requiring symptomatic pharmacological therapy.

[b00023] 2. Case Report
At nine months, her lower limb strength had returned to full power in all muscle groups except ankle dorsiflexion, which remained at MRC Grade 3. She continued physiotherapy and was referred to occupational therapy for a nighttime ankle foot orthosis.

[b00024] 2. Case Report
A timeline from diagnosis to discharge and follow‐up has been illustrated in Table 1.

[b00025] 2. Case Report
The combination of an acute painful lumbar syndrome with a predominantly dense unilateral foot drop raised several diagnostic possibilities, which were considered and excluded as follows.

[b00026] 2. Case Report
A compressive L5‐S1 radiculopathy or lumbar disc herniation was the initial working diagnosis, given the preceding back pain and the degenerative changes seen on imaging. However, the noncontrast MRI of the lumbosacral spine did not show neural compression proportionate to a complete (MRC Grade 0) foot drop.

[b00027] 2. Case Report
A compressive common peroneal palsy at the fibular head, for example, from prolonged bed rest or leg positioning during the acute illness, could not be entirely excluded and may have been contributory; however, it does not account for the preceding dermatomal pain, the CSF pleocytosis, or the positive VZV PCR.

[b00028] 2. Case Report
Other causes of lumbosacral plexopathy were considered unlikely. There was no biochemical evidence of diabetes mellitus, making an associated lumbosacral radiculoplexoneuropathy improbable. A neoplastic or infiltrative process was not supported, given the absence of constitutional symptoms, normal hematological and CSF cytology results, and clinical improvement after acyclovir and rehabilitation. An acute inflammatory neuropathy such as Guillain–Barre syndrome was also unlikely, as the deficit was strictly focal and asymmetric, and the CSF showed lymphocytic pleocytosis rather than albuminocytological dissociation.

[b00029] 2. Case Report
Finally, a bacterial, tuberculous, or fungal meningitis was considered because of the reduced CSF‐to‐serum glucose ratio, but CSF culture was negative. The multiplex meningitis/encephalitis PCR panel was negative for all six bacterial targets and for Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii. CSF AFB smear was negative. AFB culture was not performed due to insufficient sample volume. Tuberculous meningitis was in any case considered unlikely given the absence of fever or constitutional symptoms, the absence of tuberculosis risk factors, the acute rather than subacute course, the only mildly reduced glucose ratio (0.47), and the detection of an alternative pathogen in both CSF and skin.

[b00030] 2. Case Report
The detection of VZV DNA in both the CSF and a vesicle swab, together with the clinical response to acyclovir, confirmed and supported VZV as the sole identified etiology.

[b00031] 2. Case Report
The NCS/EMG at 3‐month follow‐up localized the lesion to the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head with sciatic nerve involvement rather than to a lumbar nerve root, supporting a predominantly peripheral process rather than root compression.

[b00032] 3. Discussion
This case illustrates VZV reactivation presenting as meningoradiculitis with an evolving sciatic and common peroneal neuropathy in an immunocompetent elderly woman, initially mimicking a mechanical lumbar polyradiculopathy. Although VZV reactivation usually presents as a painful dermatomal vesicular eruption (herpes zoster), motor complications are relatively uncommon and are easily missed when the rash is delayed or absent (zoster sine herpete).

[b00033] 3. Discussion
The initial clinical syndrome was most consistent with VZV‐associated meningoradiculitis, given the severe radicular pain preceding the rash, dermatomal zoster eruption, lower motor neurone pattern weakness affecting different muscle groups in the left leg, inflammatory CSF abnormalities, and detection of VZV DNA in the CSF.

[b00034] 3. Discussion
A literature review identified only seven previously reported cases of VZV‐associated sciatic neuropathy with common peroneal neuropathy (Table 2). Although such motor involvement is classically described in immunocompromised patients, it also occurs in immunocompetent individuals [–], and immunosenescence is thought to increase this risk in older adults. In a recent cohort of patients with VZV DNA detected in the CSF, the neurological syndromes and outcomes were heterogeneous [].

[b00035] 3. Discussion

EMG: electrophysiological testing was consistent with radiculitis | Treated with intravenous acyclovir and immunoglobulins and stopped immunosuppressants. At five months, pain and sphincter issues resolved, but motor deficit was unchanged

[b00042] 3. Discussion
The neurological complications of VZV are broad, ranging from postherpetic neuralgia to meningoencephalitis and myelitis. Motor involvement, termed zoster paresis or segmental zoster paresis, occurs in a minority of patients [–]. In our patient, an acute lower back pain radiating to the leg preceded the rash and led to an initial diagnosis of musculoskeletal strain, consistent with reports that zoster radiculopathy can present with dermatomal pain before the rash and be confused with compressive lumbar disease [].

[b00043] 3. Discussion
The rash may also be atypical. Leo et al. described a 79‐year‐old woman with sciatica and foot drop followed several days later by an atypical petechial rash in the L4‐L5 distribution, underscoring that both the timing and the morphology of the rash may be nonclassical in VZV‐related sciatic neuropathy [].

[b00044] 3. Discussion
A limitation of our case is the use of noncontrast lumbosacral MRI. Even though the appearance of mild degenerative changes and the mismatch between these findings and the severe neurological deficit had prompted further investigations, use of contrast‐enhanced MRI could have potentially revealed enhancement of affected nerve roots, plexus, or peripheral nerves. This would enable a better characterization of the full extent of the neuroanatomy being affected. This is supported by a previous report showing that contrast‐enhanced MRI can demonstrate nerve root or sciatic nerve enhancement in segmental zoster paresis [].

[b00045] 3. Discussion
Neurophysiological testing was deferred during the acute admission for practical and infection control reasons. This is relevant because NCS/EMG performed within the first one to two weeks may be normal or nonlocalizing before denervation is established. The NCS/EMG for our patient at three months nonetheless confirmed a severe left common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head with sciatic nerve involvement, without electrophysiological evidence of L5 radiculopathy, supporting a predominantly peripheral distribution of established injury rather than root compression.

[b00046] 3. Discussion
Herpes zoster radiculopathy that mimics disc herniation both clinically and electrophysiologically has also been described in a previous case report []. Similar patterns have been described in case reports of segmental zoster paresis and VZV‐associated lumbosacral radiculoplexoneuropathy [, ], where initial radicular pain and imaging findings are followed by electrodiagnostic evidence of plexus or peripheral nerve involvement. We postulated that the initial severe radicular pain in our patient signified the meningeal and nerve root inflammation in the early phase of illness. The subsequent NCS/EMG had only revealed the residual, predominantly peripheral component of the injury and not the initial polyradiculitis after the completion of the course of acyclovir. This final localization with predominantly peripheral nerve involvement also reflects the distribution of established axonal injury, rather than excluding possible earlier proximal or root‐level inflammation.

[b00047] 3. Discussion
The profound foot drop reflects the pathophysiology of VZV reactivation in the dorsal root ganglion, with spread to the ventral roots, anterior horn cells, or plexus, producing inflammatory neuritis, demyelination, or neuronal loss. VZV neurotropism can also cause vascular invasion, leading to ischemic neuropathy or perineuritis []. Severe lumbosacral VZV involvement can present as sciatica with motor loss and even hemi‐cauda equina syndrome []. Corticosteroids have been combined with antivirals to limit this inflammatory response in some reports, although our patient recovered with intravenous acyclovir alone.

[b00048] 3. Discussion
The 14‐day course of intravenous acyclovir was selected according to our institutional protocol for VZV infection involving the nervous system. Across reported cases, early antiviral therapy with supportive neurorehabilitation is consistently emphasized, although outcomes vary and residual deficits are common. The early intravenous acyclovir and rehabilitation produced early gait improvement despite residual weakness in our patient. She had persistent ankle dorsiflexion weakness (MRC Grade 3) at nine months follow up, requiring continued physiotherapy and ankle foot orthosis. This underscores that even with timely treatment, VZV infection can result in long term focal deficits, as reported in cases of segmental zoster paresis [].

[b00049] 3. Discussion
In summary, VZV should be considered in patients with acute radicular pain and focal motor deficits that are disproportionate to imaging, even when a rash is absent or delayed. Early antiviral therapy may limit irreversible damage and aid recovery, although residual weakness and neuropathic pain can persist.
